10027-the-triple-alliance-its-trials-and:
Harold Avery's school story follows a triple alliance of boys at Ronleigh College, beginning with a new boy and a clash with the Philistines. The alliance survives discomfiture, a supper club, catching a Tartar, and a gunpowder plot, all in the cheerful code of school fiction.

Later chapters bring third-form oratory, a holiday adventure, a screw loose in the sixth, the Wraxby match, and school elections. Avery writes for boys with high spirits and fair play. Readers get the classic boarding-school tale: friendship, mischief, sport, and the small triumphs that feel enormous at fourteen.
11372-the-nine-tenths:
James Oppenheim's 1911 novel The Nine-Tenths, dedicated to his father's memory, follows working New York through a printery, a hat factory, and a fire on East Eighty-First Street. Part one, The Dream, introduces Myra and Joe, Marty Briggs, and Joe Blaine's men; part two, The Test, follows the nine-tenths. others like Sally Heffer and Theodore Marrin, forty-five treacherous men, a fight, an arrest, a trial, and a workhouse, ending in confident morning and the city.

Oppenheim opens with hat-factory girls darting out for coffee and sandwiches, crowding a frail elevator with grimy pressmen, while oil-soaked cotton waste lies unnoticed in a dark corner. The novel's socialism is earnest: the nine-tenths who labor deserve the city they build. It remains a vivid document of Progressive-era labor fiction.
13942-brave-men-and-women-their-struggle:
O. E. Fuller published Brave Men and Women in 1884 as a book of inspiring lives. Its motto urges readers to find their fit work, labour hard at it, and keep a brave, honest heart. Chapters cover Benjamin Franklin, Sir Walter Scott and his mother, and Abigail Adams. Franklin's Poor Richard addresses taxes and thrift in homely wisdom.

Fuller defends Franklin against charges of meanness, quoting James Parton's answer. Scott's mother's education and domestic love shape her son's training. Adams appears as wife of the second president and mother of the sixth. The book mixes biography with moral exhortation. It suits readers who enjoy Victorian uplift and short lives.
14809-the-origin-and-deeds-of-the-goths:
Jordanes, a Christian Goth writing in 551, probably in Constantinople, recorded the origin and deeds of the Goths in his Getica. Charles C. Mierow's English version, part of a Princeton doctoral thesis in 1908, puts that story into English for the first time.

Mierow notes that readers who love the romance of history will enjoy a great tale of a lost cause, and will not mind the simple-hearted exaggerations of a eulogist of Gothic kings. From northern origins through migrations, battles and kingdoms, the narrative follows a people who shaped late Roman Europe. The translation remains a standard door into early Gothic history.
15774-ishmael-or-in-the-depths:
A long melodrama by Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth, author of The Hidden Hand and Self-Raised. A. L. Burt Company issued it in New York in handsome cloth at sixty cents. Southworth, a queen of popular romance, builds her tale on secrets, love, and fortune. Ishmael, a youth from the depths, rises through a world of plots and passions.

Hidden birth, lost kin, and rival lovers drive the huge plot through scene after scene. Virtue suffers, villainy schemes, and love at last finds its reward. Southworth writes with speed and feeling, never letting the reader rest. The novel charms as classic dime-novel romance: grand, tearful, and full of surprises at every turn.
16996-two-old-faiths:
J. Murray Mitchell and Sir William Muir wrote these 1891 essays on the religions of the Hindus and the Mohammedans, issued by the Chautauqua Press in New York. The essays were picked from the Present Day Tracts of the Religious Tract Society in London and reprinted by leave. A note warns that the Chautauqua council's recommendation does not mean approval of every principle in the book.

Mitchell and Muir set out Hindu and Muslim beliefs in outline, with chapters on gods, rites, and laws, from a Christian missionary standpoint. Their tone is earnest and scholarly for its day. The book gives a period survey of two great faiths, useful for history of religion, though modern readers will prefer later, insider accounts for depth and fairness.
18638-ideal-commonwealths:
Henry Morley edited this 1890 volume for Routledge's Universal Library, gathering five classic visions of a perfect state. It holds Plutarch's Lycurgus, Thomas More's Utopia, Francis Bacon's New Atlantis, and Tommaso Campanella's City of the Sun, with a fragment of Joseph Hall's Mundus Alter et Idem. Morley's introduction sets out Plato's Republic as the model behind them all.

Each work pictures a city ruled by fixed laws, shared goods, or wise guardians, yet each differs sharply in temper and detail. Read together, they show how writers across ages used an ideal city to judge their own times. The volume is a handy one-book tour of utopian thought.
22420-the-book-of-nature-myths:
The Book of Nature Myths retells tales that explain the natural world. Its opening story begins long ago, when the earth was very young. Two hunters travel through a forest far from home.

They have tracked a deer for many days by then. Night falls, dark and gloomy, around the hunters. Then a bright light comes in the western sky. Such a moment launches a myth of sky or star. The collection gathers such explanatory stories for young readers. Each tale answers a child's question about nature with a story. It preserves folk imagination in simple, clear retellings meant to be read aloud.
22518-quaint-epitaphs:
Quaint Epitaphs gathers curious inscriptions from gravestones into one book. Its compiler trusted readers would not call the book presumptuous. Many epitaph collections already existed when she published hers.

Requests for a look at her private collection prompted publication. Friends asked to examine it so often that printing followed. Graveyard verses preserve humor, grief, and local character in stone. A good epitaph can sum up a life in four lines. The compiler's haul comes from churchyards near and far. Readers get to wander cemeteries without leaving their chairs. The book charms by turns: funny, pious, odd, and sometimes deeply touching in brevity.
22693-a-book-of-myths:
A Book of Myths retells the great stories of Greek and other ancient myth for general readers. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Retellings of this era aimed to give children and busy adults the tales of gods and heroes in clear, handsome prose, with the worst crudities softened.

The sample's opening passage wrestles honestly with the gods' bad behavior. It wonders how heroes who fell fighting by the Scamander came to be worshipped as more than men. Such reflections frame the stories of Troy and Olympus that follow. The book belongs to the shelf of myth handbooks that formed the classical imagination of English-speaking readers. It still offers a graceful first path into the old tales.
23164-the-creature-from-cleveland-depths:
Fritz Leiber kicks a television in The Creature from Cleveland Depths. Gusterson gives the dead television a sour kick on his way past. If the company had use for them, he grumbles, it would pay them something. Wrong, his friend answers. Money never was the right goad for inner-directed men like Gussy, straight from the Motivations chief's own mouth.

Leiber sets his satire in a burrowed future Cleveland, where underground life runs on motivational jargon and gadgets that manage their owners. The creature of the title grows out of that managed world, part pet, part product, all consequence. Fay and Gussy argue their way through it in Leiber's wittiest register. The story predicts wearable masters with unnerving cheer, and remains very funny about a future that arrived on schedule.
24737-the-children-of-odin-the-book-of-n:
Padraic Colum wrote this book of northern myths, illustrated by Willy Pogany, retelling the Norse sagas for children. His rich, musical voice captures the magic of Asgard, the northern paradise of gods and goddesses before the dawn of history. All-Father Odin walks among men by way of the Rainbow Bridge.

Odin gives his right eye for a drink from Wisdom's well, Thor's hammer defends Asgard, and Loki's cunning turns him to treachery against the gods. Giants, dragons, dwarfs, and Valkyries crowd the tales, toward the last battle that destroyed their world. Young readers get a masterful telling of Norse myth.
2549-the-doom-of-the-griffiths:
Elizabeth Gaskell builds this Welsh tale around the traditions of Owen Glendower, the hero still loved by Welsh peasants, and a family shadowed by an old curse. The Griffiths of North Wales carry a doom that seems to follow their name from father to son.

Pride, violence, and a fatal inheritance drive the story toward its grim close, while Gaskell grounds the horror in real Welsh places and lore. The tale is short, dark, and full of the atmosphere of the hills. Readers get a folk tragedy that shows how a family's past can harden into fate.
26292-the-star-hyacinths:
James H. Schmitz's science-fiction story opens with a great unsolved crime: the robbery of the Dosey Asteroids shipping station. Raiders took six months of gem star hyacinths, worth near a hundred million credits, and seventy-nine station workers died. Most wounds were dealt to corpses, as if to hide a stranger disaster, and the dome locks had been opened from within.

Six years later, on a bleak, uncharted world, two wrecked ships lie near a lake arm. A lone man gazes at a star hyacinth whose brilliance burns his sight, and searchers spot smoke rising near the wrecks. Names such as Leed Farous, Duomart, and Dr. Egavine enter as the mystery of the gems and the dead station starts to close.
28222-due-west-or-round-the-world-in-ten:
Maturin M. Ballou's Due West, or Round the World in Ten Months, third edition, Boston, 1885, reports a ten-month circuit of the globe. Ballou, quoting De Belloy that travel abroad teaches love of home, argues that seeing the world turns cold book facts into living knowledge. His preface praises travellers who see clearly and feel deeply.

The narrative moves from port to port, with notes on peoples, cities, and customs, in the brisk style of a veteran travel writer. Ballou had already made his name with books of travel and adventure. The volume offers a lively Victorian tour of the world before air travel shrank it.
29118-the-terror-from-the-depths:
Sewell Peaslee Wright published this science fiction story in Astounding Stories in November 1931. Commander John Hanson, a space service officer, narrates the tale. His first officer Correy, a man who loves a fight, grumbles that the universe has grown quiet and that he might quit for a passenger liner.

Excitement arrives in the form of a denizen of the watery world Hydrot, an appalling creature Hanson must challenge. Wright sets a space crew against a monster of the deep, swapping the usual alien planet for an ocean world. Readers get a pulp adventure of command, courage, and a commander facing a terror rising from alien waters.
33639-the-subspecific-status-of-two-cent:
E. Raymond Hall and Keith R. Kelson revise the classification of two Central American sloths in this short 1952 paper from the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History. Two forms previously treated in the literature as separate species receive new name combinations, with evidence supporting their reduction to subspecific rank. Research assistance came through a contract between the Office of Naval Research and the University of Kansas.

The paper discusses, among others, a three-toed sloth from eastern Panama and northwestern Colombia, first named by Goldman in 1913 from only a few specimens. By comparing type localities and characters, Hall and Kelson place such forms within broader species. The study is a concise example of mid-century mammal taxonomy, where small specimen series and careful comparison reshaped species boundaries.
33754-terry-s-trials-and-triumphs:
J. Macdonald Oxley follows a poor boy toward a naval career in this 1900 boys' book. Terry's trials begin with a rough-and-tumble fight watched by a ring of ragged youngsters. In it the smaller Terry, inferior in size and weight to his opponent Mike, wins sympathy and shows vigor and agility that make up for his deficiencies. Twelve chapters carry him from a poor start through uneven going, perils by the way, and service aboard the Minnesota.

Hampton Roads, a great naval combat, adventures ashore, friends, reinstatement, and a strait betwixt two lead to an ending where all is well. Illustrations show a gallant ship sinking and driving her crew to the spar deck, and Miss Drummond fainting as she is lifted aboard. Oxley writes sturdy, patriotic adventure for young readers who enjoy sea stories and plucky heroes.
34273-gleanings-in-graveyards-a-collecti:
Gleanings in Graveyards is a collection of curious epitaphs, compiled and edited by Horatio Edward Norfolk. The hosted copy is the second edition, published in London in eighteen sixty one. Norfolk was honorary secretary to a Chelsea athenaeum, as the title page states. He dedicates the book to Robert Hunt, keeper of mining records, in thanks for kindness.

Epitaphs are sorted by place, with England first and Wales and Scotland after. Verses and inscriptions copied from stones give humour, pride, grief, and odd local fact in the dead's own billed words. Such collections served parlour reading and local history at once. Each short stone text is a tiny life story, chosen for its strangeness or charm.
36167-mirror-of-the-months:
Mirror of the Months is a small book on the turn of the year, printed in London in 1826. Its Latin motto claims it aims to please and teach at once. The writer grants that two like books came first, one by Doctor Aikin and his son, and one by Leigh Hunt, but holds that his plan stands apart.

Those books, he says, treat country things alone, one as a dry list made from old lists, the other as bright gleams on picked themes. His mirror, by contrast, is a calendar of the events and sights of each month as he saw them himself. Twelve parts, one for each month from January on, track the change of season in town and field alike.
37811-rambles-with-john-burroughs:
R J H De Loach wrote Rambles with John Burroughs, issued at Boston by Richard Badger in 1912, with photographs by the author. He gave the little volume to the dear old University of Georgia and her noble faculty. The chapters treat the simple life, around Slabsides and the den, Burroughs in the South, around Roxbury, the old clump, Burroughs as poet, Burroughs and Walt Whitman, and Burroughs and the birds.

The pictures show Burroughs in the old barn, at the study Slabsides, hearing the cardinal in Georgia, and under a Catskill ledge where he had often sheltered from summer rain. A print marks the stones of Thoreau's cabin site. De Loach writes as a disciple who walked with the old naturalist, and his book gives a near view of Burroughs at home among his hills, fields, and birds.
39532-curious-epitaphs:
Curious Epitaphs is a gathering of odd gravestone verses, collected and edited with notes by William Andrews. It first appeared in 1883 and soon went out of print; this fuller form came from Hull in May 1899. Andrews gave the book to the memory of Cuthbert Bede, author of Verdant Green, in thanks for past help and kindness.

The contents sort the verses by trade and kind: tradesmen, soldiers and sailors, musicians and actors, sportsmen, and parish clerks. Punning epitaphs and Manxland verses get their own heads. The first tradesman shown is a watchmaker of Lydford, whose verse calls integrity the mainspring of his life and prudence its regulator. Andrews mixes humour with a real love of churchyard lore.
42375-chincha-plain-weave-cloths:
O'Neale and co-authors studied these Chincha plain weave cloths of Peru. California Press issued the study in its Anthropological Records, 1949. The Chincha collection was dug in 1900 by Max Uhle there. Phoebe Hearst funds backed that Peruvian expedition of Uhle.

Contents treat the material, its sizes in length and width first. Yarns, textures, weaving means, and stitchery follow in the study. Patching, pattern, and color take sections before a summary close. Nine plates and a map of Chincha environs aid the report. The study sold at fifty cents in its records issue from the university press.
42402-horse-laughs:
Chas H Marshall drew and wrote a small book of hunting jokes called Horse Laughs. The sketches first ran in Judy, whose editor Gilbert Dalziel lent leave to print. A boy tells a local preacher to lengthen his stirrups and shorten his face. Caption jokes in broad dialect fill the pages throughout.

A late huntsman slurs praise of hounds, horses, and men in thick speech. A tenant prices a lord's new wife at tuppence ha'penny a pound above the rest. Fox, falls, and proud masters each take their comic turn. Sporting readers gain a pocket book of stable-yard wit from its day.
42634-funny-epitaphs:
Funny Epitaphs is a set of graveyard verses collected by Arthur Wentworth Eaton, in an edition of 1902. The Mutual Book Company published the book at Boston that year, copyrighted in 1885. Mottoes from Richard the Second and from Macbeth head the title page of the volume. 

An old American epitaph opens the set of epitaphs on men in the book. Under this sod and under these trees lieth the body of Samuel Pease, it runs in its lines. He is not in this hole, but only his pod, the verse goes on in its jest. He shelled out his soul and went up to God, it concludes for the reader. Eaton gathers the comic stones of two countries: puns, trades, and boasts in rhyme. The little book is a tour of churchyards by their funniest monuments, a Victorian parlour amusement with a graveyard chill in it.
43491-an-introduction-to-the-study-of-th:
An Introduction to the Study of the Maya Hieroglyphs, by Sylvanus Griswold Morley, is Bulletin 57 of the Bureau of American Ethnology at the Smithsonian Institution. The Government Printing Office in Washington issued it in 1915. The bureau's letter of transmittal, dated January 1914, recommends Morley's memoir for publication.

The letter states the book's claim plainly. The hieroglyphic writing built by the Maya of Central America and southern Mexico was probably the foremost intellectual achievement of pre-Columbian times in the New World. The earliest inscriptions now known date from about the beginning of the Christian era. Yet the glyphs are already so complex that the system must have taken many centuries to grow. Morley's introduction taught a generation of students how the signs, numbers and calendars of that writing fit together.
43495-around-the-world-in-seven-months:
Around the World in Seven Months, by Charles Gillis, is a private travel narrative. Gillis had it printed in 1891 by the Knickerbocker Press at New York. He left New York on September 8, 1889, by vestibule train westward bound. Chicago in twenty four hours, then the Rock Island route carried him on.

A burned bridge at Ogden held him two days on the way west. Yokohama, Tokio, and Nikko open the dated letters from abroad in the book. Hong Kong, Canton, Singapore, Colombo, and Calcutta follow across Asia in turn. Benares, Agra, Delhi, and Bombay lead to Suez and Cairo pyramids. Jerusalem, Jaffa, and Constantinople close the seven month circuit.
46288-stories-from-northern-myths:
Stories from Northern Myths is a retelling of Norse legend by Emilie Kip Baker. Macmillan issued it in New York in 1914. Baker had written tales of old Greece and Rome before. The book is dedicated to Sarah Homans. Its first chapter tells how all things began. Land of Mist and Land of Fire face a deep gulf there. Odin's search for wisdom follows.

The story of the magic mead comes third. Gods and men, then Sif's golden hair, follow. A guide to hard names closes the volume. Its index gives the sounds of each name. Such retellings brought the Eddas to school readers. The myths of Thor and Loki fill its pages. Baker keeps the old tales plain and grave. Young readers met the North through books like this.
46336-seven-mohave-myths:
Seven Mohave Myths, by Kroeber, is a volume in the Anthropological Records of the University of California. It was issued at Berkeley in August 1948, priced at a dollar and a quarter. The myths fill pages 1 to 70 of the volume, in phonetic spelling.

A note explains the marks used for Mohave sounds, from long vowels to a stroked l. Photographs name the tellers and helpers: Jack Jones served as interpreter for the work. Bluebird narrated the Cane story, and Jo Nelson narrated the Mastamho story. The contents give the Cane narrative first, with its song scheme and an outline of its movement. Other myths treat Vinimulye-patse, Nyohaiva, and Raven. Kroeber weighs gaps and slips in each telling as a scholar of the tribe's lore.
51062-new-lights-on-old-paths:
New Lights on Old Paths is a story and parable book by Charles Foster, author of the Story of the Bible. It was published at Philadelphia with copyright in eighteen eighty five and holds three hundred fifty illustrations, as the title page boasts. A contents list names dozens of short pieces. The Innkeeper opens the book, followed by tales of brooks, mills, and farms.

A court house steeple, a weedy farm, and a king seeking content all serve as moral pictures. Animals such as a lark, an owl, and grasshoppers speak in fable form. Foster's method is to draw a faith lesson from a common scene. Picture and tale together aimed the book at family and Sunday reading.
52112-chats-on-autographs:
Chats on Autographs, by Broadley, stands in the Books for Collectors set beside chats on china, furniture, prints, silver, costume, lace, and miniatures. Fisher Unwin published the volume in London in 1910, with one hundred and thirty-five pictures. A frontispiece shows a signed letter of William Wilson, an actor of the Fortune Theatre, to Edward Alleyn of Dulwich, dated 1620.

A motto from an old catalogue heads the book: an autograph collection may be made an admirable adjunct to the study of history and biography. Broadley also wrote on Johnson and Thrale, and on Napoleon and the invasion of England. His chats treat how to gather, judge, and house signed letters and documents, with facsimiles for the eye. The tone is that of the whole set: a connoisseur talking shop to a new collector.
5636-winding-paths:
Gertrude Page wrote Winding Paths as a novel about Dudley Pritchard, a hard-working London architect, and his lively young sister Hal. Fifteen years separate them, and Dudley views with alarm Hal's friendship with Lorraine Vivian, a fully fledged actress. He disapproved of Lorraine from their first meeting, for no particular reason, as he disapproved of many things without troubling to find out why.

Hal, still a hoydenish schoolgirl, understands her brother far better than he understands her, finding humor in his self-congratulatory tolerance. The novel follows siblings, theatre folk, and London society. Readers get an engaging Edwardian story of family, judgment, and young independence.
56851-shakspeare-s-mental-photographs:
Hurd and Houghton of New York issued this parlour game book in 1866, with E P Dutton of Boston. Its mottoes come from Hamlet and King Lear, on holding the mirror up to nature and on speaking truth. The game rests on ten questions, each with twenty answers, and every answer is a line from Shakespeare.

The questions ask what you are, what traits you prize in others, your favourite pursuit, and your pet dislike. Later ones ask your first greeting, your chief wish, and your future. One player keeps the book and asks in order. The person asked picks any number from one to twenty, and the matching quote gives the mental photograph. It turns Shakespeare into a fortune game for the drawing room.
57004-the-trossachs:
Mitton wrote The Trossachs, a guide in the Beautiful Britain series from Black of London in 1911. The line holds like books on Abbotsford, Cambridge, the English Lakes, and Windsor. Contents open with The Lady of the Lake, the poem that made the region famed. The royal city of Stirling and the route of the Fiery Cross to Balquhidder follow. Approaches to the Trossachs and the heart of the Trossachs take the middle chapters.

Loch Lomond and the MacGregors close the text, and an index ends the book. Plates show birches by Loch Achray, the crags of Ben Venue, and Stirling Castle. Loch Katrine with Ellen's Isle, Ben A'an, and the head of Loch Lomond aid the eye. Mitton says the name Trossachs is said to mean bristled territory.
57521-the-junior-classics-volume-2-folk-:
William Patten selected these folk tales and myths for young folks. Collier printed Junior Classics volume two in New York in 1912. A Parrish plate, Ah, Naughty Pandora, fronts the tales here. Stories from northern sagas open the volume in first place.

How all things began and gifts from the queen of sky follow. Thor journey to Jötunheim and his lost hammer tale appear next. Iduna apples of youth and the chained Fenris wolf come on. Balder the beautiful and Brunhilda and Siegfried fill later pages. A reading guide by Professor Neilson of Harvard aids the young folks shelf set.
58217-the-book-of-months:
Benson, author of Scarlet and Hyssop and Mammon and Company, wrote this book of months, published by William Heinemann at London in 1903 and dedicated to his mother. The contents divide the volume by the calendar, January through December, each month with its own long entry. The publisher adds a note correcting a statement about a disinfectant on page eighty-three.

January opens on thick yellow fog, with electric light needed to dress and breakfast by, and the narrator watches Oxford Street from his window as the fog lifts into primrose sunshine. London, he says, holds forty-eight hours in every twenty-four, since no one can sit idle there or even read a book. Ten yards of Piccadilly, he declares, is a volume, and the Circus an improper epic, and the journal of a London year begins.
58904-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
An index of the Project Gutenberg works of Edgar Rice Burroughs lists his tales. David Widger compiled the index for readers of the online set. Some two dozen book titles stand in the contents at the front. Mars tales, Tarzan tales, and lost-world tales crowd the long list. Clicking a mark by a title opens that book's own contents list.

A Princess of Mars opens the Mars line of his famed books. The Gods of Mars and Warlord of Mars carry that line onward. Thuvia, Maid of Mars and Chessmen of Mars stand later in it. Tarzan of the Apes heads the jungle line of the index here. The Beasts of Tarzan and Jungle Tales of Tarzan follow in order. At the Earth's Core and Pellucidar open the hollow-earth line of tales. The index lets a reader jump to any chapter of any book.
58993-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of John Burroughs maps the naturalist's many books. Widger compiled the index. It lists more than twenty Burroughs volumes. Each volume's table of contents is printed in full. Wake-Robin and Winter Sunshine stand among the first. Whitman, a study of the poet, stands among the last.

The contents pages show Burroughs's range plainly. Birds and bees fill the early papers. Sharp eyes and pastoral bees recur as titles. The Adirondacks and the Catskills supply his ground. One volume camps and tramps with Roosevelt. Another treats time and change through a geologist's eyes. Hawaii holidays and the spell of the Yosemite widen the map. The index lets a reader survey the whole shelf at a glance.
59396-the-boy-travellers-in-south-americ:
The Boy Travellers in South America is a travel adventure book by Thomas Knox. Harper issued it in New York in 1886. Two youths tour the continent in the tale. Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia stand early on the route. Brazil, Paraguay, and Argentina follow. Chile and the far south close the circuit. Voyages on the Amazon and La Plata rivers fill large parts.

Knox wrote a whole series of such boy travellers books. The Far East set ran to five volumes. Japan, Siam, Ceylon, Egypt, and Africa each had their book. The Vivian's polar voyage was a mate to these. Heavy illustration was a mark of the series. The books taught geography through a story frame. Young readers toured the world without leaving home. This volume covers the southern continent in full.
61352-the-case-against-spirit-photograph:
Case Against Spirit Photographs is an inquiry by Patrick and Whately Smith, published in London in 1921. Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner and Company issued the book from Carter Lane that year. Contents divide the case between the two authors in the chapters. An introductory chapter by Smith and a historical chapter by Patrick open the volume.

Fraud is the third chapter, in three parts, in the contents of the book. General methods, experiments in fraud, and internal evidence of fraud are its heads in the list. The reliability of witnesses, the value of recognition, and recent literature come after in order. Real test conditions close the shown chapters of the inquiry. The authors did what conjurors do in their tests. They made spirit photographs themselves, and showed the seams. Their years were the years when Cottingley and the war dead filled the journals.
62805-new-tablecloths:
A book of crochet cloths for the table fills this small work, printed in 1948. It is the fifty-seventh Star Book of the American Thread Company, and cost ten cents. The first leaf of cuts praises its theme: blooms are the choice of all, and these cloths of blooms in thread are sure to be the choice of the home. A cloth of blooms lets fine ware and plate show at their best, it says.

The first cloth in the book is a cloth of the poinsettia bloom. Its needs are set out in full: balls of the Star thread of the house, of a set size and count, in cream, dun, or white. A steel hook of a set size is named as well. Each small tile of the work spans a set width.
6376-self-raised-or-from-the-depths:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth opens Self Raised, or From the Depths, with recovery and a verse on hope darkened by doubt. Ishmael, parted from Claudia in anguish, will not long succumb to despair, for his strength of intellect and will holds him, and Bee's love holds him too. Bee has loved him since school, through country teaching and law study, and loves him now as a successful barrister, while Claudia's power to desolate his life has limits.

Chapters run from Herman and Ishmael and second love through Woodside and Tanglewood. A professor of odd jobs, a journey, and Lady Vincent's reception follow. Romance and reality, Castle Cragg, Faustina, and a plot against Claudia follow, with a judge sailing from Boston on the Oceana and Ishmael agreeing to go, whatever sacrifices it costs. Southworth writes melodrama with moral force, where a self raised man rises by work and loyalty.
65398-the-calumet-book-of-oven-triumphs:
The Calumet Book of Oven Triumphs is a baking book put out by the General Foods Corporation under a 1934 copyright, as form 516. It sells Calumet, the double acting baking powder, through recipes. A close picture shows a slice of Calumet cake.

What makes a perfect cake, the book asks. Even rising, a tender brown crust, delicate flavor and fragrance, it answers. All these qualities and one more, the fine, moist, tender texture that is hard to describe by any word except velvety. Velvety crumb is the expression cake judges use for cakes leavened by Calumet. Every Calumet cake, plain or party, dark or light or golden yellow, has this same lovely texture. Thanks go to Calumet dependable double action. Cooks get a brand recipe book of the Depression years.
6561-our-friend-john-burroughs:
Clara Barrus writes of John Burroughs as a friend, not just as a writer of books on birds and fields. Her chapters follow him from his farm boyhood and family life to his days at Slabsides, his winter walks, and his camps with John Muir. Sketches of his early work sit beside warm, close glimpses of the man himself.

Barrus notes how praise in a man's own time can feel uneasy, and how true worth shows only with years. Yet her tone stays fond, not stiff, as she recalls talk, walks, and quiet hours outdoors. Our Friend John Burroughs gives a personal portrait of a poet of nature, seen by one who knew him well.
66072-woodland-paths:
Woodland Paths is a volume of nature essays by Winthrop Packard, published in Boston by Small, Maynard and Company in 1910. Charles Copeland illustrated it. The book belongs to a set of four volumes called The New England Year. Wild Pastures, Wood Wanderings, and Wildwood Ways complete the seasons.

Packard thanks the Boston Transcript for leave to reprint pieces first written for its columns. The opening essay, South Rain, sets the tone of close seasonal watching. A plate shows six ducks swinging over the author's head in rosy dusk. Each volume of the set sold separately in ornamental cloth with gilt top. Together they walked the reader through a New England year outdoors. Packard wrote gentle, exact nature prose for city readers who walked woods on Sundays.
70318-indian-nature-myths:
Julia Darrow Cowles wrote Indian Nature Myths for the Flanagan company at Chicago, copyright 1918, with illustrations by Dorothy Dulin. Twenty-three short tales, each tagged with its tribe, explain the natural world for child readers. The Ojibwa give How the Seasons Came to Be and the Birth of the Arbutus. The Iroquois give the Origin of the Violet and How Mosquitoes Came to Be, and the Chippewa the Gift of Indian Corn. Others come from the Blackfeet, Algonquin, Shoshonee, Shawnee, and Passamaquoddy.

The first tale follows Omeme, little son of Ojeeg the Fisher, mightiest hunter of his tribe. Omeme wants game, but finds the birds flown to the sun and the creatures hid under the snow. Cowles also wrote Stories to Tell for the same school market. The tales are retold simply, in the manner of school nature readers.
7291-the-two-paths:
John Ruskin's Two Paths gathers five lectures on art and its power over nations. They open with the deteriorative power of conventional art. Then they move through the unity of art, modern manufacture and design, the influence of imagination in architecture, and the work of iron in nature, art, and policy. Appendices and a list of illustrations, from the ideal of an angel to the serpent beguiling Eve, support the text.

Ruskin argues that art shapes a people's character for good or ill, and that honest making beats empty ornament every time. His lectures, spoken at different times yet linked by design, preach with a prophet's heat and a craftsman's eye. The book remains a fierce, eloquent plea for truth in art and work.
74419-reuben-sachs:
Amy Levy wrote Reuben Sachs, a sketch issued by Macmillan in London and New York in eighteen hundred eighty eight. Levy had won note for The Romance of a Shop. Reuben is the pride of a rich Jewish house in Lancaster Gate. His mother and sister wait for his return in the first scene.

Reuben shone at school and won a grant to the university. At the bar his name rose fast in his first years. A hard lost vote for a seat drew fresh eyes to him. Then strain broke his health all at once. Doctors sent him on a long sea trip to the far south. They warned that Jews fill half their nerve lists. Reuben jokes that his race pays for high culture yet lives long.
75684-a-century-of-excavation-in-the-lan:
A Century of Excavation in the Land of the Pharaohs is a work by James Baikie on the digging up of ancient Egypt. It holds thirty-two plates made for the volume. Baikie was the author of works on the tales and kings of the ancient world and on the lands of the Bible. A portrait statue of Thothmes III in the Cairo Museum stands as the first picture.

The contents trace a hundred years of work in the field. The first chapter tells of the pioneers, and the second of Mariette and his work. Later chapters take up the pyramids and their explorers, work among the temples, and buried royalty. A chapter on Tutankhamen stands late in the list as shown. The book is a survey of Egyptology in the field, told in the order of its finds.
78705-out-of-the-depths:
Mrs Madeline Leslie wrote a novel subtitled the rector's trial, copyrighted in 1879 at Boston and dedicated to her precious little ones by their loving grandmother. Leslie had written Home Life and Tim the Scissors Grinder. A motto from David heads the title: out of the depths have I cried to thee, O Lord. Chapter one is sunset, chapter two retrospection.

The rector's trial of the subtitle is a trial of faith and reputation. Ira Bradley published the book as successor to Henry Hoyt. Leslie, the pen name of Harriet Baker, wrote dozens of evangelical tales. Her volumes filled Sunday school libraries across America.
9250-a-book-of-autographs:
Hawthorne's Book of Autographs considers a volume of letters, chiefly by soldiers and statesmen of the Revolution, addressed to General Palmer, himself a swordsman for the cause. They suit a quiet afternoon, withdrawn from the present, when a reader can glide back three quarters of a century and stand amid ominous circumstances.

Imagine the letters just brought by a splashed postrider or a hurried dragoon, Hawthorne urges, and they become magic scrolls. The sketch meditates on handwriting as character. It remains a charming essay on history made personal by ink and paper.
9855-classic-myths:
Mary Catherine Judd, principal of the Lincoln School in Minneapolis, retold Classic Myths for young readers, with pictures by Angus MacDonall drawn from classic sources. Tales span Greek, Norse, Roman, German, Finnish, and Russian lore. The sun's horses, Woden of the northern sky, and Jupiter of the southern sky open the set. Diana, Jack and Jill on the moon mountains, and the man in the moon follow.

Later myths tell how fire came to earth, why rivers hold gold sands, and how Echo, Iris, and Neptune rule air and sea. Judd writes with plain clarity for school use. A reader gets a wide, gentle book of world myths, fit for reading aloud and first wonder.
a-book-of-autographs: Nathaniel Hawthorne introduces a collection of autographs chiefly from soldiers and statesmen of the Revolution. The letters are addressed to General Palmer, himself a soldier in the cause, and invite quiet reading far from present day concerns. Hawthorne asks readers to imagine the troubled times in which the writers lived and wrote. The book thus turns old letters into a window on the mood of the Revolutionary age.
brave-men-and-women-their-struggles-fail:
Osgood Eaton Fuller published Brave Men and Women with an 1884 copyright, gathering lives under one motto: find your fit work and keep a brave, honest heart. Fuller writes short lives for home reading, each built on struggle, failure, and triumph. Franklin opens the roll at fifty-two, still climbing.

Abigail Adams, Horace Greeley, and Wendell Phillips carry the American chapters. Sir Walter Scott and his mother show the home school behind fame. Sir John Franklin dies a martyr of the polar sea, and Chinese Gordon fights in Crimea, China, and the Soudan. Garfield's maxims, a Quaker courtship, and talks on wives and husbands fill the gaps. Fuller's set is uplift by example, plainly told for family shelves.
britannica-1911-acroliths:
Acroliths were statues built from two materials at once. The word comes from Greek words meaning ending in stone. The trunk of such a figure was wood. The head, hands, and feet were marble. This mixed construction marks a transition period. It stands between early wooden images and full stone sculpture. Gilding often concealed the wooden trunk. Drapery concealed it even more commonly. Only the marble parts showed to viewers.

Examples come from travel writing. Pausanias mentions acroliths frequently in his descriptions. The best known specimen stood at Plataea. It was the Athene Areia of the Plataeans. Readers gain a clear picture of the technique. Cheap, light wood formed the hidden body. Costly marble formed every visible extremity.
britannica-1911-aurochs:
Aurochs is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on the extinct wild ox of Europe. Its name joins the Latin word urus with the plain word ox. When the beast died out, its name passed to the bison by mistake. A German writer of the fifteen hundreds is the key source.

His book on Muscovy, printed at Venice in 1550, shows both kinds. Its woodcuts show the aurochs and the bison as two clear types. He had seen both alive on his trips through Poland, it seems. The last aurochs was killed in a Polish forest in 1627. Its hue is given as black in his account of the beast.
britannica-1911-autographs:
Autograph is a term with three uses. It can mean a paper signed by the man from whom it comes. It can mean a paper written out in full by that man's own hand. Or it can mean a plain signature on its own. Such papers must be as old as writing itself. The early papyri of Egypt may hold some.

The habits of the East make that less likely, the piece argues. Paid scribes wrote the body of most state papers. A seal did the work of a signature. Its print was the sign that gave the paper force. Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name and sealed them with his seal. Scribes, of course, held the pen. Darius is said to have signed a decree in the same sealed sense. The long piece goes on to the care, study, and trade of such relics.
britannica-1911-nymphs:
Nymphs, in Greek myth, are a large host of female powers of low rank. They stand for the powers of nature that make and tend new life. The 1911 Britannica entry hunts for the root of the word. One guess ties it to the word for cloud, with the sense of veiled. A bride was led veiled to her new home, and the term grew from that use.

Their home, the entry says, is on hills and in groves. They haunt springs and rivers, vales and cool caves. They walk in the train of great gods and goddesses. Among them are the huntress, the seer god, and the god of wine and trees. Rough gods of flock and field walk with them too. The kinds of nymph are sorted by the sphere each one haunts, from the sea to the woods.
britannica-1911-rare-earths:
Rare Earths is a chemistry article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a set of metal oxides found together in a few rare minerals. The metals look much alike in how they act with other matter. For ease, the article splits them into three groups: the cerium group, the terbium group, and the ytterbium group. It lists each metal with its sign and its atomic weight as then known.

The cerium group holds scandium, yttrium, lanthanum, cerium, and others up to samarium. The terbium group holds europium, gadolinium, and terbium, and the third runs from dysprosium through to lutecium. Though the metals are very rare, a large count of minerals hold them. They turn up chiefly in Scandinavia, parts of the Urals, America, and Australia, most often in very old rocks. The entry is a snapshot of a field still being sorted out, name by name.
britannica-1911-vlachs:
The Vlachs, a Latin people of south east Europe, are described in a 1911 Britannica article. They are spread wide both north and south of the Danube. Their range runs from the Bug River in Russia to the Adriatic Sea. Their total count is put at ten or eleven million.

North of the Danube most Vlachs dwell in Rumania and Transylvania. Near a million more live in Bessarabia and south Russia. South of the river, near half a million are scattered over north Greece and Turkish lands. The piece warns that exact counts are not to be had in lands where race and rule are so mixed. Some writers put the total as low as nine million.
britannica-1911-wainewright-thomas-griff:
Thomas Griffiths Wainewright (1794-1852) was an English journalist and painter, and his bright start and dark turn fill an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Chiswick and educated by a distant relative, he began a literary life in 1819. He wrote for several magazines under playful pen names.

The entry ties him above all to the London Magazine, where his smart, flippant art criticism ran from 1820 to 1823, and counts Charles Lamb among his friends. He also showed figure pictures at the Royal Academy. Ruined by extravagant habits, he insured his sister-in-law's life for 18,000 pounds in 1830, and when she died that year the offices refused to pay.
c-f-meyer-die-hochzeit-des-monchs:
A monk leaves his monastery for love, and the consequences unfold like a dark fairy tale in C. F. Meyer's Die Hochzeit des Moenchs, given here in German. The Monk's Wedding is framed as a story told at Dante's tomb in Verona, which lends the telling a solemn music. Passion stands against vows throughout the novella.

The frame's listeners interrupt, question, and darken the tale as it proceeds, a device Meyer handles beautifully. Medieval atmosphere thickens around a very modern psychology of desire and guilt. The monk's choice echoes outward until no one in the story stands untouched. Haunting is the word readers reach for with this one. It shows the master's late manner at full strength.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-cloths:
Altar cloths cover the altar during the Mysteries, as St. Optatus of Mileve notes in the fourth century. A law attributed to Boniface III in the seventh century made the covering obligatory, and three cloths became customary probably in the ninth, now strictly required for a licit Mass. The rule guards against spilt Precious Blood reaching the altar stone, since the cloths absorb it first.

Formally cloths were gold and silver cloth set with stones, silk, and other rich material, but now only linen or hemp may be used. The two lower cloths have to cover the whole table, length and width, whether one folded piece or two distinct pieces. The top cloth stays single and reaches the predella on both sides. Celebrating without a cloth is a grievous offence except in grave necessity, such as Sunday Mass or Viaticum for the dying.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andechs:
Andechs is a Benedictine monastery and pilgrimage place on a hill east of the Ammersee in Upper Bavaria. Its site first held a castle of the counts of Diessen, probably Roman. Pilgrimage fame dates from 955. Relics Saint Rasso had brought from Rome and the East to Worth were moved here to escape the Huns.

In the twelfth century three Sacred Hosts joined the relics. Two were reputedly consecrated by Gregory I, one by Leo IX. Andechs became Der heilige Berg, the holy mountain. A thirteenth-century Andechs missal in Munich gives the earliest mention of the Hosts. Duke Ernest raised a collegiate church in 1438. Duke Albert III turned it into a Benedictine monastery in 1455, with monks from Tegernsee. It became an abbey in 1458. Prosperity ran until secularization in 1803. In 1850 it rose again as a Benedictine priory under Munich's Saint Boniface abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casimir-ubagh:
Casimir Ubaghs was born at Bergélez-Fauquemont in November 1800 and died at Louvain in February 1875. For a quarter century he led the Ontologico-Traditionalist School of Louvain. After teaching philosophy at Rolduc, he moved to Louvain in 1830, and the school became a center of Ontologism under him. In 1846 he took over the Revue catholique, the school's official journal, with Arnold Tits and Lonay, drawing followers such as La Forêt, Claessens, Bouquillon, and Van Loo.

Opponents led by Kersten's Journal historique et littéraire fought the Revue for years, with the fiercest controversy from 1858 to 1861. The Index had already flagged five propositions in 1843 and ordered corrections Ubaghs misunderstood. A Roman Congregation decision of September 1864 censured a series of his Ontologism propositions, ending his career. His books include a natural theology in four editions, anthropology texts, and an 1860 essay on ontological ideology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-english-post-:
English post-Reformation oaths are the subject of this entry, which explains why the Crown demanded them. Since the Reformation was imposed from above, submission to its key formulas was exacted by oath, test, or formal declaration, and the formulas shifted with the moods of those in power. The oath of royal supremacy, imposed in March 1534, stands first.

The title Supreme Head had entered a convocation decree in February 1531 and met stiff clerical resistance, since it might later gain a religious sense it did not yet carry. On the advice of Fisher and Warham, the clergy submitted after adding the saving words, as far as God's law allows. Two years later Parliament declared the king the only supreme head on earth of the Church of England. Fisher and More would accept the succession of Anne Boleyn's children but refused the supremacy, and paid for that refusal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu:
Johann Nepomuk Fuchs was a Bavarian chemist and mineralogist whose name still attaches to soluble glass. Born in 1774, he first studied medicine, then turned to chemistry and mineralogy at Heidelberg, Berlin, Freiburg, and Paris. He taught at Landshut and Munich, joined the Academy of Sciences in 1823, and became conservator of Munich's mineral museum in 1854.

His best-known discovery, published in 1823, was water glass, an alkaline silicate used in a kind of fresco painting called stereochromy and later in surgical bandages. He also worked on cement, the artificial production of ultramarine, beet sugar, brewing, and dyeing, and a chromium-bearing variety of muscovite was named fuchsite after him. His collected works appeared at Munich in 1856, the year of his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oaths:
An oath, in moral theology, asks God to stand witness to a statement’s truth, directly by his name or indirectly by creatures that show his majesty. Swearing by heaven, the cross, or the Gospels counts as tacit invocation, and every oath needs at least a virtual intent to invoke God's testimony.

The entry sorts oaths into assertory, affirming past or present fact, and promissory, binding a future resolve, vow, or pact. Contestatory oaths merely invoke witness, imprecatory ones add a curse on falsehood, and the entry weighs when oaths bind, when they excuse, and when they sin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ostrogoths:
The Ostrogoths were one of the Goths' two chief tribes, a Germanic folk. Their oldest homes on record stood on the right bank of the Vistula. About the middle of the second century they moved, in whole or in part, to the Black Sea lands between the Don and Danube. From there they raided Greek and Asian cities and fought Romans and neighbour tribes without rest.

Emperor Decius fell against them in 251, and after defeat by Claudius in 269 they held Dacia from Aurelian. United under Ermanaric from 350 to 375, they fell to the Huns, then won freedom when Attila's empire broke in 453. Theodoric later ruled Italy with Roman law, art, and letters, tolerant toward Catholics though Arian himself. His kingdom fell in a long war, and the last Ostrogoth fortress fell in 555.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-special-devot:
Special devotions for months grew out of the slow separation of popular prayer from the official liturgy. And this entry explains the shift and then lists the devotions month by month. In the Middle Ages laity joined the daily psalmody, Mass. And processions and knew the liturgy well, while extra practices like the Rosary, a stand-in for the 150 Psalms, still sprang from liturgical roots.

From the sixteenth century onward, unliturgical practices took their own course, with Stations of the Cross, Forty Hours, litanies, novenas, and series of Sundays for particular saints or mysteries. Whole months came to belong to one devotion, January to the Holy Name of Jesus among them, and the entry pairs each month's devotion with its indulgences.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-griffi:
Thomas Griffiths, Vicar Apostolic of the London District, was born in London in 1791 and died in 1847, the only holder of that office educated wholly in England. Sent to St. Edmund's College, Old Hall, at thirteen, he was ordained in 1814 and chosen president at twenty-seven, ruling the college with success for fifteen years. Consecrated Bishop of Olena in 1833, he succeeded Bishop Bramston three years later.

His years in office saw the first stirrings of the hierarchy's restoration and the subdivision of England's four districts into eight in 1840. The Oxford conversions followed, with Newman a Catholic nearly two years before Griffiths died. Irish immigration after the potato famine forced many new missions, and Pugin's revival of Christian art was gathering pace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-visigoths:
The Visigoths were one of the two principal branches of the Goths, sharing history with the Ostrogoths until 375. Ulfilas laboured among them, translated the Bible into their tongue, and preached Arianism with great success until Prince Athanaric forced him to withdraw in 348. At the Huns' invasion some fled with Athanaric to Transylvania's mountains, but most appealed to Emperor Valens to enter the Roman Empire.

In 376 some 200,000 Visigoths crossed the Danube, revolted against oppressive governors, plundered the country, and defeated and killed Valens near Adrianople in 378. Theodosius made peace in 382, seeking to unite them with the empire through national commanders and to reconcile Arians with Nicene Christians. After his death in 395 they elected Alaric of the Baltha family king. Sought a Germanic kingdom on Roman soil, invaded the Balkans to the Peloponnese in 396, and entered Italy in 401.
classic-myths:
Classic Myths, by Mary Catherine Judd, retells sky, weather, and nature myths for young readers and teachers. Each tale in the contents is tagged by its source people: Greek, Roman, Norse, German, Russian, or Finnish. Star stories lead: Jupiter of the southern sky, Diana queen of the moon, and the Great Bear.

Fire, wind, and rainbow tales follow: How Fire Came to Earth, A Bag of Winds, Echo the air maiden, and Iris the rainbow princess. Flower and tree tales close the list, from the gift of the olive tree to the girl changed into a sunflower. Suggestions to teachers, a bibliography, and a pronouncing index equip the book for classroom use.
govdocs-archive_org-KlausFuchs_Klaus_Fuc: An FBI records-review inventory sheet for the New York files logs the bureau's holdings on Klaus Fuchs. Fuchs was the physicist who spied for the Soviet Union from inside the atomic bomb project. Review sheets record what a file holds and where its parts were sent, here between the Bureau and Albuquerque among others. He confessed in 1950. The sheet is pure paperwork: declassified inventory from the handling of the Cold War's most damaging espionage case.
ideal-commonwealths:
Henry Morley edited this set of classic plans for a perfect state, issued in London in 1890. The book holds Plutarch on Lycurgus, More's Utopia, and Bacon's New Atlantis. It also holds Campanella's City of the Sun and a fragment by Hall. Morley wrote the long introduction.

Each work sets out laws, work, learning, and rule for an ideal land. Sparta's strict training sits near More's shared goods and Bacon's house of science. Readers can weigh the plans side by side in one volume. The set shows how long writers have dreamed of a just and ordered common life.
ishmael-or-in-the-depths:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth wrote Ishmael, or In the Depths, a long popular novel issued at New York. Ishmael is the hidden hero whose rise the tale tracks. A school scene in the middle praises a boy who won honors by three years of hard study. Temptation and rest were denied, the speaker marvels, for months and years.

Do not envy him until you have matched his effort, boys are told. Poverty, secret birth, and patient merit shape Ishmael's path. Southworth's list of companion novels fills the front pages, from The Hidden Hand onward. The book is her best-known tale of rags to honor.
our-friend-john-burroughs:
Clara Barrus, physician and devoted friend of the naturalist John Burroughs, assembled Our Friend John Burroughs as a contemporary tribute rather than a posthumous life. Its contents mix her own framing with his autobiographical sketches. Ancestry, childhood, self-analysis, and the early writings appear. So do a winter day at his Slabsides cabin, and camping with John Muir.

Everyone claims Burroughs as a friend, Barrus begins, because he is blended with our love of birds, flowers, and the outdoors. Against the obituary method of appreciation — wait until the daisies have bloomed over a man for decades — she offers familiar glimpses now, from readers who walked and listened beside him. The book preserves the poet-naturalist as his own generation knew him.
self-raised-or-from-the-depths:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth wrote this long novel of a lowly hero raised by his own worth. Contents run past thirty-eight chapters, moving from Recovery and Father and Son through journeys, storms, and a shipwreck. Names in the chapter heads include Herman, Ishmael, Bee, and Claudia.

Plots against Claudia, a night of horror in a castle vault, and a rescue late in the book promise rich sensation. Southworth blends love, pride, and hidden birth in the lush style her serial readers loved. The tale rewards patience with reversals at every turn, as worth wins out over rank and malice.
the-doom-of-the-griffiths:
Elizabeth Gaskell's tale The Doom of the Griffiths grows from Welsh lore about Owen Glendower. Gaskell opens with her own love of North Wales traditions and notes that Glendower lives in folk memory as much for magic as for patriot pride. A prize poem at Oxford on his name once stirred the whole principality, she says.

At its heart stands a curse. Glendower spared a false friend who plotted his death, and doomed his line instead. The Griffiths family bears that doom down the years. Gaskell blends folk tale, history, and moral weight.
the-nine-tenths:
James Oppenheim's novel The Nine-Tenths, dated 1911 and dedicated to the memory of his father, is present here only in title page, dedication, and contents, so the story does not appear. The contents divide the novel into two parts, The Dream and The Test, each with its own numbered chapters.

Part I opens in The Printery, then turns to The East Eighty-First Street Fire and The Good People. Myra and Joe, Marty Briggs, and Last of Joe Blaine and His Men follow. Part II promises beginnings, a chapter sharing the book's title, forty-five treacherous men, a fight in good earnest, an arrest, and The Trial, with a character named Rhona entering late.
the-origin-and-deeds-of-the-goths:
Jordanes, a Christian Goth, wrote the Getica, the origin and deeds of his people, in the year 551, probably at Constantinople. Charles C. Mierow put the work into English as part of his Princeton doctoral thesis, published in 1908. A note by Andrew F. West says this is the first time the Gothic story appears in English form.

West warns that Jordanes mixes fable and legend with fact and praises his own race freely. Readers who want cold, scientific narrative, he says, should stay away. Yet he calls the tale a great story of a lost cause, and its simple-hearted exaggerations heighten rather than spoil its interest for lovers of the romance of history.
the-triple-alliance-its-trials-and-trium: Harold Avery's Triple Alliance, Its Trials and Triumphs, is a school story presented here by its contents list alone. Twenty chapters begin with A New Boy and the Philistines, then move through a supper club, catching a Tartar, a gunpowder plot, and Ronleigh College. Later headings promise the Wraxby match, elections, a reading-room riot, a cipher letter Diggory reads, and a secret society. The alliance's trials can be followed in outline here, while its members speak only beyond this record.
the-two-paths: John Ruskin's Two Paths is laid out here in a contents list and a list of illustrations, stopping at the heading of his preface. Five lectures are promised. They cover the deteriorative power of conventional art over nations, and the unity of art. Modern manufacture and design follow. So do imagination in architecture, and the work of iron in nature, art, and policy. The illustrations name an angel, the serpent beguiling Eve, and classical architecture. Ruskin's lectures are charted here, while his arguments begin past the preface heading.
two-old-faiths: Two Old Faiths offers essays on the religions of the Hindus and the Mohammedans by J. Murray Mitchell and Sir William Muir. The Chautauqua Press at New York issued the book in 1891 for the C.L.S.C. reading circles. The essays were selected from the Religious Tract Society's Present Day Tracts. The contents begin the Hindu essay with the Vedas, philosophy, and ritualism. Only the title pages and start of the contents are present here, so the essays themselves do not appear.
winding-paths: Gertrude Page's Winding Paths is represented here by its title page and a bare contents list, so nothing of the story can be seen. The contents name no chapter titles at all. Forty-three chapters are listed by number alone, from chapter one to chapter forty-three. No place, person, or event is named in the pages present. Readers learn the author's name, the book's title, and its length in chapters, and nothing more of what the paths wind through or where they lead.
